relationship: overlapping prophetic dating by named kings
rationale: Both openings place the prophetic words in the reigns of Uzziah of Judah and Jeroboam son of Joash of Israel. Hosea also lists three additional Judean kings; Amos adds the earthquake dating.
source_text: The word of the Lord that came to Hosea son of Beeri in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel.

target_units.text: The words of Amos that came among nakkarim from Tekoa, which he saw concerning Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah king of Judah and Jeroboam son of Joash king of Israel, two years before the earthquake.

relationship: parallel portrayal of Israel's unfaithfulness as prostitution
rationale: Hosea's commanded household sign explains the land's departure from the Lord as prostitution. Jeremiah likewise describes Israel's worship on mountains and beneath trees as prostitution and adultery with wood and stone.
source_text: The beginning of the Lord’s word to Hosea. The Lord said to Hosea, “Go, take for yourself a woman of prostitution and children of prostitution, for the land will utterly prostitute itself away from following the Lord.”

target_units.text: The Lord said to me in the days of King Josiah, You saw what the dwelling of Israel did to Me. They went upon every high mountain and beneath every wooded tree and prostituted themselves there.
After she prostituted herself in all these ways, I said, Return to Me. But she did not return, and faithless Judah saw her faithlessness.

I saw that, concerning all the things in which the dwelling of Israel was caught committing adultery, I sent her away and gave a certificate of divorce into her hands. Yet faithless Judah did not fear; she too went and prostituted herself.
Her prostitution came to be regarded as nothing, and she committed adultery with wood and stone.

relationship: related prophetic births bearing announced national signs
rationale: Hosea takes Gomer, who bears a son; Isaiah approaches the prophetess, who likewise bears a son. The surrounding divine naming commands give both births a sign concerning national events.
source_text: He went and took Gomer daughter of Debelaim; she conceived and bore him a son.

target_units.text: I approached the prophetess; she became pregnant and bore a son. The Lord said to me, “Call his name Plunder-quickly, Spoil-swiftly,
because before the child knows how to call father or mother, he will take Damascus’s power and Samaria’s spoils before the king of the Assyrians.”

relationship: named historical setting for Jehu and bloodshed at Jezreel
rationale: Kings records Jehu's demand for the royal sons' heads at Jezreel and his killing of Ahab's remaining household there. Hosea announces vengeance for Jezreel's blood upon Jehu's house; the comparison preserves the different judgments expressed.
source_text: The Lord said to him, “Call him Jezreel, for in a little while I will avenge Jezreel’s blood upon Jehu’s house and put an end to the kingdom of Israel’s house.

target_units.text: He wrote them a second letter, saying, ‘If you are for me and obey my voice, take the heads of the men, your master’s sons, and bring them to me at Jezreel about this hour tomorrow.’ The king’s sons were seventy men; these prominent men of the city were bringing them up.
When the letter reached them, they took the king’s sons and slaughtered them, seventy men. They put their heads in baskets and sent them to him at Jezreel.
The messenger came and reported, saying, ‘They have brought the heads of the king’s sons.’ He said, ‘Put them in two mounds beside the doorway of the gate until morning.’
In the morning he went out, stood in the city’s gateway, and said to all the people, ‘You are righteous. Behold, I conspired against my master and killed him. But who struck all these?’
‘See—Appho—that nothing of the Lord’s word that the Lord spoke against Ahab’s house will fall to the ground. The Lord has done all that He spoke through His slave Elijah.’
Jehu struck all who remained in Ahab’s house in Jezreel, all his prominent men, his acquaintances, and his priests, so that he left him no remnant.

relationship: shared image of God shattering a bow
rationale: Hosea locates the breaking of Israel's bow in Jezreel's valley. The psalm describes the Lord shattering a bow while ending wars across the earth; the shared weapon image has different stated scopes.
source_text: On that day I will shatter Israel’s bow in the Valley of Jezreel.”

target_units.text: Bringing wars to an end as far as the earth’s limits, He will shatter a bow and break a weapon apart and burn shields in fire.

relationship: later reversal of the named child's exclusion from mercy
rationale: The daughter is named Not Shown Mercy as Israel's house faces withheld mercy. The later promise expressly names Not Shown Mercy as the recipient of mercy, reversing the sign's announced condition.
source_text: She conceived again and bore a daughter. He said to him, “Call her Not Shown Mercy, for I will certainly no longer show mercy to Israel’s house, but I will surely set Myself against them.

target_units.text: I will sow her for Myself upon the land, show mercy to Not Shown Mercy and say to Not My People, ‘You are My people.’ He will say, ‘Thou art the Lord my God!’”

relationship: parallel distinction between divine rescue and military reliance
rationale: Hosea promises Judah rescue by the Lord without bows, swords, chariots or horses. Isaiah rebukes reliance on Egyptian horses and chariots instead of seeking God and declares the helpers unable to secure survival.
source_text: But I will show mercy to Judah’s sons and save them by the Lord their God. I will not save them by bow, sword, war, chariots, horses or horsemen.”

target_units.text: Woe to those going down to Egypt for help, trusting in horses and chariots because there are many, and in horses, a very great multitude, but not trusting Israel’s Holy One or seeking God!
He Himself, wise, brought evils upon them; His word will certainly not be set aside. He will rise against evil people’s houses and against their futile hope,
an Egyptian human being and not God, horses’ flesh, with no help. The Lord will bring His hand against them; the helpers will grow weary, and all will perish together.

relationship: explicit apostolic reuse of the not-My-people naming
rationale: Hosea names the son Not My People and announces the broken relationship. Paul expressly cites Hosea when describing those not God's people being called His people, presenting the naming in its promised reversal.
source_text: He said, “Call him Not My People, for you are not My people, and I am not yours.”

target_units.text: As He also says in Hosea, “I will call those who are not My people ‘My people,’ and her who is not beloved ‘beloved’;

relationship: explicit quotation of sons of the living God
rationale: Paul reproduces the promise that the place where people were called not God's people becomes the place where they are called sons of the living God. Romans places the quotation in an argument concerning those called from Jews and Gentiles.
source_text: The number of Israel’s sons was like the sand of the sea, which will not be measured or counted. In the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not My people,’ there they will be called sons of the living God.

target_units.text: and in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not My people,’ there they will be called sons of the living God.”

relationship: shared sea-sand image for the multitude of descendants
rationale: Hosea compares Israel's sons to unmeasurable sea sand. The promise to Abraham compares his multiplied seed to sand on the seashore; this connection concerns the numerical image, distinct from Hosea's restored naming.
source_text: The number of Israel’s sons was like the sand of the sea, which will not be measured or counted. In the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not My people,’ there they will be called sons of the living God.

target_units.text: surely I will bless you, and greatly multiply your seed as the stars of the heaven, and as the sand upon the shore of the sea; and your seed shall inherit the cities of their adversaries.

relationship: parallel reunification under one authority
rationale: Hosea brings Judah's and Israel's sons together under one authority. Ezekiel gathers Israel, ends the division into two kingdoms and promises one ruler, subsequently naming David.
source_text: Judah’s sons and Israel’s sons will gather together, appoint one authority for themselves and come up from the land, for great is Jezreel’s day.

target_units.text: and say to them, Thus says the Lord, the Lord: Behold, I am taking all Israel’s house from among the nations where they entered, gathering them from all those around them and bringing them into Israel’s land.
I will make them one nation in My land and upon Israel’s mountains, and one ruler will be theirs. They will no longer be two nations or ever again be divided into two kingdoms,

so that they no longer defile themselves with their idols. I will deliver them from all their lawless deeds in which they sinned and cleanse them. They will be My people, and I, the Lord, will be their God.
My servant David will be ruler among them, and one shepherd will be over all, because they will walk in My ordinances, keep My judgments and do them.

relationship: parallel reversal to peoplehood and received mercy
rationale: Hosea commands the positive names My People and Shown Mercy. Peter likewise contrasts former absence of peoplehood and mercy with being God's people and receiving mercy.
source_text: Say to your brother, ‘My People,’ and to your sister, ‘Shown Mercy.’

target_units.text: Once you were not a people, but now you are God’s people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.

relationship: related mother-and-divorce imagery for communal estrangement
rationale: Hosea calls for judgment against the mother and declares the wife-husband relationship broken. Isaiah asks about the mother's divorce document and connects her dismissal with the people's lawless acts.
source_text: “Enter into judgment with your mother, enter into judgment! For she is not My wife and I am not her husband. I will remove her prostitution from My face and her adultery from between her breasts,

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: “What is your mother’s divorce document with which I sent her away? Or to which debtor have I sold you? Behold, you were sold because of your sins, and I sent your mother away because of your lawless acts.

relationship: parallel exposure of an unfaithful woman as judgment
rationale: Hosea threatens to strip the mother naked, returning her to her birth condition. Ezekiel's judgment against personified Jerusalem likewise includes removal of clothing and leaving her naked and exposed.
source_text: so that I may strip her naked and restore her as on the day of her birth. I will make her like a wilderness, set her like a waterless land and kill her with thirst.

target_units.text: I will hand you into their hands. They will tear down your brothel, pull down your platform, strip your clothing from you, take your vessels of boasting, and leave you naked and exposed.

relationship: related generational judgment and mercy in rejected worship
rationale: Hosea extends the refusal of mercy to the unfaithful mother's children. The prohibition of other gods describes judgment reaching children and mercy toward those who love God; the family imagery and legal formulation remain distinct.
source_text: I will certainly show no mercy to her children, for they are children of prostitution.

target_units.text: You shall not bow down to them, neither shall you serve them; for I am the Lord your God, a jealous God, repaying the sins of fathers upon children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate Me,
and showing mercy to thousands, to those who love Me and keep My ordinances.

relationship: parallel attribution of material provision to rejected worship
rationale: Hosea's mother credits her lovers with bread and other necessities. Jeremiah records worshippers crediting their service to the queen of heaven with plentiful bread and well-being, and blaming abandonment of that worship for deprivation.
source_text: For their mother prostituted herself; she who bore them brought shame. She said, ‘I will follow my lovers, who give me my loaves and water, my garments and linen cloths, my oil and everything due to me.’

target_units.text: We will certainly do everything that will come from our mouths: burn incense to the queen of heaven and pour out drink offerings to her, as we, our fathers, our kings, and our rulers did in Judah’s cities and outside Jerusalem. We were filled with bread, were well off, and saw no calamities.
But when we stopped burning incense to the queen of heaven, we were all diminished and perished by sword and famine.

relationship: close imagery of divinely obstructed roads and paths
rationale: Hosea describes God blocking the woman's way and building up her roads so she cannot find her path. Lamentations likewise describes roads built up and paths blocked, in the voice of an afflicted speaker.
source_text: Therefore look, I block her way with thorns and will build up her roads, and she will certainly not find her path.

target_units.text: He built against me, and I will not go out; He made my bronze heavy.
Indeed, I will cry and call out; He blocked my prayer.
He built up my roads, blocked my paths and troubled them.

relationship: related return prompted by remembered provision
rationale: The woman resolves to return to her former husband because her earlier condition was better. The younger son likewise remembers bread in his father's household and resolves to return; the relationships and narratives differ.
source_text: She will pursue her lovers but certainly not catch them; she will seek them but certainly not find them. She will say, ‘I will go and return to my former husband, for it was better for me then than now.’

target_units.text: But when he came to himself, he said, ‘How many of my father’s hired workers have bread to spare, while I am perishing here from hunger!
I will rise and go to my father and say to him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you.
I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired workers.”’
And he rose and came to his own father. But while he was still far away, his father saw him and was moved with compassion. He ran, fell upon his neck, and kissed him tenderly.

relationship: parallel diversion of God's gifts into unfaithful worship
rationale: Hosea identifies God as giver of grain, wine, oil and silver that was turned toward Baal. Ezekiel likewise charges Jerusalem with making images from God's gold and silver and setting His food and oil before them.
source_text: She did not know that it was I who gave her grain, wine and oil and multiplied silver for her; but she made silver and gold objects for Baal.

target_units.text: You took your vessels of boasting from My gold and My silver, from what I had given you, made male images for yourself and prostituted yourself among them.
You took your patterned clothing and clothed them; you set My oil and My incense before them.
My loaves that I gave you—fine flour, oil and honey with which I fed you—you set before them as a fragrant aroma. So it happened, says the Lord.

relationship: related withdrawal of agricultural provision in judgment
rationale: Hosea announces recovery of God's grain and wine and removal of clothing. Haggai describes heaven and earth withholding provision and a sword upon grain, wine and oil; its stated setting is neglect of God's house.
source_text: Therefore I will return and recover My grain at its season and My wine at its time; I will take away My garments and linen cloths so that they do not cover her shame.

target_units.text: therefore heaven will hold back dew, and the earth will withhold its produce.
I will bring a sword upon the land and the mountains, upon grain, wine and oil, and whatever the earth produces, upon people and livestock, and upon all the labors of their hands.”

relationship: parallel exposure before the woman's lovers
rationale: Hosea threatens to uncover the woman's uncleanness before her lovers. Ezekiel likewise gathers Jerusalem's lovers and promises to reveal her evils so that they see her shame.
source_text: Now I will uncover her uncleanness before her lovers, and certainly no one will deliver her from My hand.

target_units.text: Therefore behold, I am gathering against you all your lovers with whom you mingled, all whom you loved together with all whom you hated. I will gather them against you from all around, reveal your evils to them, and they will see all your shame.

relationship: parallel ending of festive rejoicing
rationale: Hosea announces the removal of rejoicings, festivals and assemblies. Amos announces festivals turned to mourning and songs to lamentation, sharing the reversal of communal celebration under judgment.
source_text: I will turn away all her rejoicings, her festivals, new moons and Sabbaths, and all her festal assemblies.

target_units.text: I will turn your festivals to mourning and all your songs to lamentation. I will put sackcloth on every waist and baldness on every head; I will make him like mourning for a beloved one, and those with him like a day of pain.

relationship: parallel devastation of vine and fig trees
rationale: Hosea threatens the vine and fig trees that the woman credited to her lovers. Joel describes a destructive nation laying God's vine waste and shattering His fig trees; the shared crops are ruined in differently described judgments.
source_text: I will obliterate her vine and fig trees, of which she said, ‘These are my wages that my lovers gave me.’ I will make them a testimony, and the field’s beasts, heaven’s birds and the earth’s creeping things will devour them.”

target_units.text: For a nation has come up against My land, strong and uncountable. Its teeth are a lion’s teeth, and its grinding teeth a young lion’s.
It laid My vine waste and shattered My fig trees; searching, it searched it out and cast it away; it whitened its branches.

relationship: close juxtaposition of ornaments and forgetting God
rationale: Hosea describes the woman putting on earrings and necklaces while following lovers and forgetting God. Jeremiah asks whether a bride will forget her adornment, then contrasts God's people forgetting Him.
source_text: “I will exact vengeance upon her for the days of the Baalim, when she sacrificed to them, put on her earrings and necklaces and went after her lovers, but forgot Me,” says the Lord.

target_units.text: Will a bride forget her adornment, or a virgin her breastband? Yet My people forgot Me for days beyond counting.

relationship: shared speaking-to-the-heart language in a communal address
rationale: Hosea says God is leading her astray, will place her in a wilderness and speak to her heart. Isaiah directs priests to speak to Jerusalem's heart and comfort her; the comparison concerns that address without replacing Hosea's unusual opening wording.
source_text: “Therefore look, I am leading her astray; I will place her in a wilderness and speak to her heart,

target_units.text: Comfort, comfort My people, says God.
You priests, speak to the heart of Jerusalem; comfort her. For her humiliation is fulfilled, her sin is loosed; for from the hand of the Lord she has received double for her sins.

relationship: named Achor setting in restoration promises
rationale: Hosea promises possessions and the Valley of Achor to open understanding. Isaiah promises a resting place for cattle in Achor's ravine for God's people who sought Him; the same named place receives distinct favorable uses.
source_text: and from there I will give her her possessions and the Valley of Achor to open her understanding. There she will be humbled as in the days of her infancy and the days of her ascent from Egypt’s land.

target_units.text: There will be shelters for flocks in the woodland, and the ravine of Achor will be a resting place for cattle, for My people who sought Me.

relationship: related restored relationship expressed through wife imagery
rationale: Hosea promises the address My Husband in place of Baalim. Isaiah speaks of the Lord and a wife while promising mercy after abandonment; it does not supply Hosea's change of divine address.
source_text: On that day,” says the Lord, “she will call Me ‘My Husband’ and no longer call Me ‘Baalim.’

target_units.text: “The Lord has not called you like an abandoned, fainthearted wife, nor like a wife hated since youth,” says your God.
“For a short time I abandoned you, and with great mercy I will have mercy on you.
In a little anger I turned My face from you, and with everlasting mercy I will have mercy on you,” says the Lord who rescued you.

relationship: close promise to remove and forget idols' names
rationale: Hosea promises removal of the Baalim's names from the woman's mouth and an end to their remembrance. Zechariah likewise announces destruction of idols' names from the land so they are no longer remembered.
source_text: I will remove the names of the Baalim from her mouth, and they will certainly no longer remember their names.

target_units.text: On that day, says the Lord, I will destroy the idols’ names from the land, and there will no longer be remembrance of them. I will remove the false prophets and the unclean spirit from the land.

relationship: parallel covenant safety concerning beasts and settled hope
rationale: Hosea promises a covenant involving animals, an end to weapons and settlement in hope. Ezekiel's covenant of peace removes harmful beasts and promises dwelling in hope without terror; the arrangements are differently stated.
source_text: On that day I will establish a covenant for them with the field’s beasts, heaven’s birds and the earth’s creeping things. I will shatter bow, sword and war from the land and settle you in hope.

target_units.text: I will make a covenant of peace with David and remove harmful beasts from the land. They will dwell in the wilderness and sleep in the woods.
I will place them around My mountain and give you rain, rain of blessing.

The trees in the plain will give their fruit, and the land will give its strength. They will dwell upon their land in hope of peace and know that I am the Lord when I shatter their yoke. I will rescue them from the hand of those who enslaved them.
They will no longer be plunder for the nations, and the land’s beasts certainly will no longer eat them. They will dwell in hope, and no one will terrify them.

relationship: related enduring mercy within a restored covenant relationship
rationale: Hosea promises everlasting betrothal characterized by righteousness, mercy and compassion. Isaiah promises everlasting mercy and a covenant of peace that will not be removed, within its wife imagery.
source_text: I will betroth you to Myself forever; I will betroth you to Myself in righteousness and judgment, in mercy and compassion,

target_units.text: “For a short time I abandoned you, and with great mercy I will have mercy on you.
In a little anger I turned My face from you, and with everlasting mercy I will have mercy on you,” says the Lord who rescued you.
“This dates for Me from the water in Noah’s time, when I swore to him then concerning the earth not to be angry with you again, nor at a threat against you
for mountains to move away; nor will your hills be shifted. So neither will My mercy toward you fail, nor will your covenant of peace ever be removed.” For the Lord said, “I am gracious to you.”

relationship: parallel restored relationship marked by knowing the Lord
rationale: Hosea's faithful betrothal culminates in knowing the Lord. Jeremiah's new-covenant promise likewise joins the restored God-and-people relationship with universal knowledge of Him among its recipients.
source_text: and I will betroth you to Myself in faithfulness, and you will know the Lord.

target_units.text: Because this is the covenant I will make with Israel’s house after those days, says the Lord: I will surely put My laws into their understanding and write them upon their hearts. I will be their God, and they will be My people.

And they will certainly not teach each his fellow citizen or his brother, saying, Know the Lord, because they will all know Me, from their least to their greatest. I will be merciful toward their injustices and certainly remember their sins no more.

relationship: contrast between responsive and withholding heaven and earth
rationale: Hosea describes God listening to heaven and heaven listening to earth. Haggai describes heaven withholding dew and earth withholding produce; the comparison concerns linked heaven-earth provision, without adding dew to Hosea's clause.
source_text: On that day,” says the Lord, “I will listen to heaven, and heaven will listen to the earth,

target_units.text: therefore heaven will hold back dew, and the earth will withhold its produce.

relationship: shared grain-wine-oil triad in renewed provision
rationale: Hosea's chain of listening includes earth, grain, wine, oil and Jezreel. Joel expressly promises grain, wine and oil to satisfy God's people, giving the same three products in a restoration setting.
source_text: and the earth will listen to grain, wine and oil, and they will listen to Jezreel.

target_units.text: The Lord answered His people: “Look, I am sending out to you grain, wine and oil, and you will be filled with them. I will no longer give you over to reproach among the nations,

relationship: explicit quotation adapting restored peoplehood and favor
rationale: Paul identifies Hosea as the source of the promise to call those not God's people His people. Hosea's mercy naming is accompanied in Romans by not-beloved and beloved language, which should not be made verbally identical.
source_text: I will sow her for Myself upon the land, show mercy to Not Shown Mercy and say to Not My People, ‘You are My people.’ He will say, ‘Thou art the Lord my God!’”

target_units.text: As He also says in Hosea, “I will call those who are not My people ‘My people,’ and her who is not beloved ‘beloved’;

relationship: related renewed divine attachment despite Israel's unfaithfulness
rationale: Hosea's command to love an adulterous woman expressly compares God's love for Israel despite foreign gods. Jeremiah calls estranged Israel to return, declares God's mercy and promises to bring the withdrawn children to Zion.
source_text: The Lord said to me, “Go again and love a woman who loves evil things and is an adulteress, just as God loves Israel’s sons, though they look toward foreign gods and love cakes with raisins.”

target_units.text: Go and read these words toward the north: Return to Me, dwelling of Israel, says the Lord. I will not set My face firmly against you, because I am merciful, says the Lord, and I will not be angry with you for ever.
Only recognize your injustice: you acted ungodly toward the Lord your God and spread your ways to strangers beneath every wooded tree, but you did not obey My voice, says the Lord.
Return, children who have withdrawn, says the Lord, because I will rule over you. I will take you, one from a city and two from a clan, and bring you into Zion,

relationship: related exclusive and reciprocal marital claims
rationale: Hosea requires the woman to remain with him without prostitution or belonging to another man and adds his own reciprocal clause. Paul likewise speaks of each person's own spouse and reciprocal marital obligations; the settings and formulations differ.
source_text: I said to her, “You will remain with me many days; you must certainly not prostitute yourself or belong to another man, and I toward you.”

target_units.text: But because of cases of sexual immorality, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband.
Let the husband fulfill his obligation to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband.
The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.

relationship: parallel loss of ruling and religious institutions
rationale: Hosea anticipates many days without king, ruler, sacrifice, altar, priesthood or manifestations. Lamentations describes king and rulers among the nations, no law and prophets without vision, a related deprivation with a different list.
source_text: For Israel’s sons will remain many days without king or ruler, without sacrifice or altar, without priesthood or manifestations.

target_units.text: Her gates were fixed in the earth; He destroyed and broke her bars. Her king and her rulers are among the nations. There is no law; even her prophets saw no vision from the Lord.

relationship: close promise of restored Israel under David
rationale: Hosea anticipates Israel seeking the Lord and David their king. Ezekiel promises David as ruler over the reunited people and continuing residence in their land; neither comparison requires identifying a later historical individual.
source_text: After these things Israel’s sons will return and seek the Lord their God and David their king; they will be astonished at the Lord and His good things in the last days.

target_units.text: My servant David will be ruler among them, and one shepherd will be over all, because they will walk in My ordinances, keep My judgments and do them.
They will dwell upon their land, which I gave My servant Jacob, where their fathers dwelt. They will dwell upon it, and David My servant will be their ruler for ever.

relationship: parallel divine case against Israel
rationale: Hosea opens the accusation with the Lord's case against the land's inhabitants and names missing truth, mercy and recognition. Micah likewise announces the Lord's case against His people and His argument with Israel.
source_text: Hear the Lord’s word, sons of Israel, for the Lord has a case against the land’s inhabitants: there is no truth, no mercy and no recognition of God upon the land.

target_units.text: Hear, hills, the Lord’s judgment, and you ravines, foundations of the earth! For the Lord has a case against His people, and He will argue it with Israel.
“My people, what have I done to you? How have I grieved you, or how have I troubled you? Answer Me!

relationship: close catalogues of murder, theft and adultery
rationale: Hosea lists cursing, falsehood, murder, theft and adultery overflowing the land. Jeremiah's temple accusation likewise names murder, adultery, theft and unjust swearing, then adds worship of foreign gods.
source_text: Cursing, falsehood, murder, theft and adultery have poured over the land, and they mix bloodshed with bloodshed.

target_units.text: and murder and commit adultery and steal and swear unjustly, and you burned incense to Baal and followed foreign gods whom you do not know, to your own harm,

relationship: close judgment extending to people, beasts, birds and fish
rationale: Hosea describes the mourning land and loss affecting its inhabitants, beasts, birds and sea fish. Zephaniah likewise announces disappearance of humanity, livestock, sky birds and sea fish.
source_text: Therefore the land will mourn and diminish with all who inhabit it, with the field’s beasts, the earth’s creeping things and heaven’s birds; the sea’s fish will disappear,

target_units.text: Let everything utterly disappear from the face of the earth, says the Lord,
let humanity and livestock disappear, let birds of the sky and fish of the sea disappear, and I will remove people from the face of the earth, says the Lord.

relationship: parallel priestly failure concerning knowledge and law
rationale: Hosea connects rejection from priestly service with thrusting away recognition and forgetting God's law. Malachi says priests should guard knowledge and law, then condemns their departure and announces their dishonor.
source_text: My people were likened to one without knowledge. Because you thrust away recognition, I too will thrust you away from serving Me as priest. You forgot your God’s law, and I too will forget your children.

target_units.text: For a priest’s lips will guard knowledge, and people will seek law from his mouth, because he is the messenger of the Lord Almighty.
But you have turned aside from the way and weakened many through the law; you have corrupted the covenant of Levi,” says the Lord Almighty.
“And I have made you despised and neglected among all the nations, because you did not guard My ways but showed partiality in the law.”

relationship: related loss or exchange of glory through unfaithfulness
rationale: Hosea says God will turn the sinners' glory into dishonor. Jeremiah charges God's people with exchanging their glory; the connection concerns lost glory, while the stated agents and actions differ.
source_text: According to their multitude, so they sinned against Me; I will turn their glory into dishonor.

target_units.text: Will nations exchange their gods, though these are not gods? But My people exchanged their glory, from which they will not benefit.

relationship: related priestly eating and sin vocabulary
rationale: Hosea accuses the priestly group of eating the people's sins and taking their souls amid injustices. Leviticus permits the offering priest to eat a sin offering; the comparison distinguishes that regulated offering from Hosea's condemnatory language.
source_text: They will eat My people’s sins and take their souls amid their injustices.

target_units.text: Speak unto Aaron and his sons, saying: This is the law of the sin offering. In the place where they slaughter the whole burnt offering, they shall slaughter the offerings for sin before the Lord; they are most holy.
The priest who offers it up shall eat it. It shall be eaten in a holy place, in the court of the Tent of Testimony.

relationship: close leveling of priest and people in judgment
rationale: Hosea declares that it will be with the priest as with the people and promises repayment. Isaiah likewise places people and priest together among the ranks affected by the Lord's announced destruction.
source_text: It will be as with the people, so with the priest; I will exact punishment upon him for his ways and repay him for his schemes.

target_units.text: The people will be like the priest, the slave like the master, the maidservant like the mistress; the buyer will be like the seller, the lender like the borrower, and the debtor like the one to whom he owes a debt.
The earth will be utterly destroyed, and the earth utterly plundered, for the Lord’s mouth has spoken these things.

relationship: close judgment of eating without satisfaction
rationale: Both passages state that the judged people will eat but not be filled. Hosea connects the failure with abandoning fidelity to the Lord; Micah places it among announced blows for sins.
source_text: They will eat but certainly not be filled; they prostituted themselves but will certainly not prosper, because they abandoned keeping faith with the Lord.

target_units.text: You will eat but certainly not be filled. It will grow dark within you and turn aside, and you will certainly not be saved; whoever is saved will be handed over to the sword.

relationship: related association of wine and sexual imagery
rationale: Hosea joins prostitution, wine and intoxicating drink in the people's receptive heart. Proverbs warns about lingering over wine and then describes eyes seeing another woman and a mouth speaking crooked things.
source_text: My people’s heart welcomed prostitution, wine and intoxicating drink.

target_units.text: Is it not those who linger over wines? Is it not those who track down where drinking parties take place?
Do not become drunk with wine, but associate with righteous people, and converse during walks; for if you give your eyes to bowls and cups, afterward you will walk about barer than a pestle.
But at the end he lies stretched out as though struck by a snake, and as though by a horned viper its poison spreads through him.
When your eyes see another woman, then your mouth will speak crooked things,

relationship: specific parallel of divination employing a rod
rationale: Hosea condemns inquiry through signs and rods amid estrangement from God. Ezekiel describes Babylon's king tossing a rod, questioning carved images and inspecting a liver; both connect rods with divinatory inquiry.
source_text: They inquired by signs, and by his rods they announced things to him; they were led astray by a spirit of prostitution and prostituted themselves away from their God.

target_units.text: For Babylon’s king will stand upon the ancient road, at the beginning of the two roads, to divine a divination, toss a rod, question the carved images and inspect a liver at his right.

relationship: close mountain-and-tree setting for unfaithful worship
rationale: Hosea describes sacrifices on mountains and hills beneath named trees and connects them with prostitution. Jeremiah likewise portrays Israel's prostitution on every high mountain and beneath every wooded tree.
source_text: On the mountaintops they sacrificed, and on the hills they offered sacrifice, beneath oak, poplar and a tree providing shade, because shelter is good. Therefore your daughters will prostitute themselves and your daughters-in-law commit adultery.

target_units.text: The Lord said to me in the days of King Josiah, You saw what the dwelling of Israel did to Me. They went upon every high mountain and beneath every wooded tree and prostituted themselves there.

relationship: related confrontation concerning adultery and one's own conduct
rationale: Hosea refuses to single out daughters and daughters-in-law while the men themselves mix with prostitutes and sacrifice with initiates. Paul asks the teacher who forbids adultery whether he commits it; the different arguments bring those addressed into examination of their own conduct.
source_text: I will certainly not call your daughters to account when they prostitute themselves, or your daughters-in-law when they commit adultery, for the men themselves mixed with prostitutes and sacrificed with initiates; the people who understood became entangled with a prostitute.

target_units.text: you then who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who proclaim that one must not steal, do you steal?
You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you rob temples?

relationship: close prohibition of entering Gilgal
rationale: Both passages explicitly prohibit entering Gilgal. Hosea addresses Judah, while Amos's surrounding call addresses Israel's house. Their other destinations differ; Hosea's house of On is not silently identified with Amos's Bethel.
source_text: But you, Israel, do not be ignorant; and Judah, do not enter Gilgal or go up to the house of On, and do not swear by the living Lord.

target_units.text: Do not seek Bethel, do not enter Gilgal, and do not cross over to the Well of the Oath; for Gilgal will certainly be taken captive, and Bethel will be as though it did not exist.”

relationship: related bovine images for Israel or Ephraim needing restraint
rationale: Hosea compares Israel to a heifer running wild. Jeremiah represents Ephraim as a calf not taught, speaking after discipline and asking to return; the shared animal image has different immediate developments.
source_text: For Israel has run wild like a heifer running wild. Now the Lord will pasture them like a lamb in an open place.

target_units.text: I surely heard Ephraim wailing: Thou didst discipline me, and I was disciplined; like a calf I was not taught. Turn me back, and I will return, because Thou art the Lord my God.

relationship: close link between idols and a stumbling block
rationale: Hosea calls Ephraim a partner of idols who set stumbling blocks for himself. The psalm says service of carved images became a stumbling block to the people.
source_text: Ephraim, a partner of idols, set stumbling blocks for himself.

target_units.text: They served their carved images, and it became a stumbling block to them.

relationship: related association with nations and prostitution through their practices
rationale: Hosea associates choosing Canaanites with prostitution and dishonor. The psalm describes mixing with nations, learning their works, serving Canaan's images and prostituting themselves through their practices.
source_text: He chose Canaanites. They prostituted themselves thoroughly; they loved dishonor arising from their arrogance.

target_units.text: and mixed with the nations and learned their works.
They served their carved images, and it became a stumbling block to them.
They sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons,
and shed innocent blood, the blood of their sons and daughters whom they sacrificed to Canaan’s carved images; the land was murdered with blood,
and was defiled by their works, and they prostituted themselves through their practices.

relationship: parallel trapping imagery in accusations against the people
rationale: Hosea addresses priests, Israel and the royal house as a trap and stretched net. Jeremiah describes impious people setting traps to catch men and compares their deceitful houses to a bird-filled trap.
source_text: Hear these things, priests; pay attention, house of Israel; listen, house of the king, for the judgment is against you. You became a trap at the lookout and like a net stretched over Itabyrion,

target_units.text: For impious people were found among My people, and they set traps to destroy men and were catching them.
Like a set trap full of birds, so their houses are full of deceit; therefore they became great and rich.

relationship: parallel divine knowledge of wrongdoing
rationale: Hosea declares that Ephraim is known and Israel is not away from God amid their defilement. Jeremiah similarly says all their ways are before God's eyes and their wrongdoings are not hidden.
source_text: I know Ephraim, and Israel is not away from Me; for now Ephraim has prostituted himself and Israel is defiled.

target_units.text: Because My eyes are upon all their ways, and their wrongdoings were not hidden before My eyes.

relationship: parallel failure of unfaithful Israel to return
rationale: Hosea says their schemes were not directed toward returning and associates this with a spirit of prostitution. Jeremiah likewise recounts Israel's prostitution followed by God's call to return and her failure to do so.
source_text: They did not direct their schemes toward returning to their God, for a spirit of prostitution is within them, and they did not recognize the Lord.

target_units.text: After she prostituted herself in all these ways, I said, Return to Me. But she did not return, and faithless Judah saw her faithlessness.

relationship: parallel humbling of arrogance
rationale: Hosea announces Israel's arrogance humbled and the weakening of Israel, Ephraim and Judah. Isaiah likewise announces humbling for the insolent, arrogant and elevated on the Lord's day.
source_text: Israel’s arrogance will be humbled before his face. Israel and Ephraim will weaken in their injustices, and Judah too will weaken with them.

target_units.text: For the Lord’s eyes are high, but the human being is low; humanity’s height will be humbled, and the Lord alone will be exalted on that day.
For the Lord Sabaoth has a day against every insolent and arrogant person, against everyone high and elevated; they will be humbled,

relationship: parallel rejected approach accompanied by animal offerings
rationale: Hosea says people will seek God with sheep and calves but not find Him because He turned away. Isaiah refuses abundant animal offerings and says God turns His eyes away from supplication amid bloodshed.
source_text: With sheep and calves they will go to seek the Lord, but they will certainly not find Him, because He turned away from them,

target_units.text: “What is the multitude of your sacrifices to Me?” says the Lord. “I am full of burnt offerings of rams; fat of lambs and blood of bulls and male goats I do not desire,
not even if you come to appear before Me. For who demanded these things from your hands? To trample My court,
you will no longer continue. If you bring fine flour, it is futile. Incense is an abomination to Me. Your new moons and sabbaths and a great day I cannot endure; fasting and idleness,
and your new moons and your festivals My soul hates. You have become more than enough for Me; I will no longer let your sins go.
Whenever you stretch your hands toward Me, I will turn My eyes away from you. Even if you multiply supplication, I will not listen to you, for your hands are full of blood.

relationship: parallel trumpet warning amid approaching judgment
rationale: Hosea commands a trumpet signal on the hills and proclamation in the house of On. Jeremiah similarly commands a trumpet over the land and urgent gathering and flight because crushing is coming from the north; the locations are distinct.
source_text: Blow a trumpet on the hills; sound out on the heights; proclaim in the house of On! Benjamin was beside himself;

target_units.text: Announce in Judah, and let it be heard in Jerusalem; say: Signal with a trumpet over the land, and cry loudly! Say: Gather, and let us enter the walled cities!
Take up and flee to Zion; hurry, do not stand still, for I am bringing evils from the north and great crushing.

relationship: legal counterpart to the image of moving boundaries
rationale: Hosea compares Judah's rulers to people moving boundaries. Deuteronomy expressly prohibits removing a neighbor's inherited boundaries, supplying a concrete legal counterpart to Hosea's accusation.
source_text: Judah’s rulers became like people moving boundaries; upon them I will pour My onrush like water.

target_units.text: You shall not remove your neighbour’s boundaries, which your fathers set in your inheritance, which was allotted unto you in the land which the Lord your God gives you for a possession.

relationship: parallel human suppression of judgment
rationale: Hosea charges Ephraim with oppressing his adversary and trampling judgment. Isaiah's confession likewise says, We drove judgment backward, and describes God's displeasure at the absence of judgment.
source_text: Ephraim oppressed his adversary and trampled judgment, because he began to follow worthless things.

target_units.text: We acted impiously and lied and withdrew from following our God. We spoke unjust things and disobeyed; we conceived and meditated on unjust words from our heart.
We drove judgment backward, and righteousness has withdrawn far away, for truth was consumed in their ways, and they could not go straight through.
Truth has been taken away, and they turned their mind away from understanding. The Lord saw, and it did not please Him that there was no judgment.

relationship: related goad image in divine confrontation
rationale: Hosea says God is like a goad to Judah's house. In Acts the voice identifying Himself as Jesus tells Saul that kicking against goads is hard; the shared image does not identify the two recipients or explain Hosea's separate turmoil clause.
source_text: I am like turmoil to Ephraim and like a goad to Judah’s house.

target_units.text: When we had all fallen to the ground, I heard a voice speaking to me in the Hebrew language: ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me? It is hard for you to kick against goads.’
I said, ‘Who art Thou, Lord?’ The Lord said, ‘I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.

relationship: later repudiation of the Assyrian help found inadequate earlier
rationale: The earlier accusation says the Assyrian king could not heal Ephraim and Judah's pain. The later confession explicitly says Assur will not save; the repeated rejection of Assyrian rescue is expressed through different images.
source_text: Ephraim saw his illness and Judah his pain; Ephraim went to the Assyrians and sent ambassadors to King Jarim. But he could not heal you, and pain will certainly not cease among you.

target_units.text: Assur will certainly not save us; we will not mount a horse, and we will certainly no longer call the works of our hands “Our gods.” The One in you will have mercy on an orphan.

relationship: shared predatory imagery with no rescuer
rationale: Hosea compares God to a panther and lion who seizes with no rescuer. Isaiah compares the approaching force to lions and describes seizing and an absence of rescue; the depicted agents differ.
source_text: For I am like a panther to Ephraim and like a lion to Judah’s house. I seize and will go away and take, and there will be no one to rescue.

target_units.text: They rush like lions and have taken their stand like a lion’s cub. It will seize and cry out as a beast does and cast out, and no one will rescue them.

relationship: close seeking and rising early toward God under affliction
rationale: Hosea says they will seek God's face and rise early toward Him in affliction. The psalm says that whenever He killed them, they sought Him, returned and rose early toward God; Hosea's opening until-they-disappear clause is not rewritten as an admission of guilt.
source_text: I will go and return to My place until they disappear; they will seek My face, and in their affliction they will rise early toward Me, saying,

target_units.text: Whenever He killed them, they sought Him; and they returned and rose early toward God,
and remembered that God is their helper, and God Most High is their redeemer.

relationship: close pairing of divine striking and healing
rationale: Hosea's call to return says God seized and will heal, and will strike and dress wounds. Eliphaz similarly says God causes pain and restores, struck and healed with His hands.
source_text: “Let us go and return to the Lord our God, because He has seized us and will heal us; He will strike and dress our wounds.

target_units.text: Happy is the person whom the Lord reproved; do not refuse the Almighty’s admonition.
For He causes pain and restores again; He struck, and His hands healed.

relationship: related third-day rising and life
rationale: Hosea's collective voice expects restored health and rising to live before God on the third day. Paul's received proclamation says Christ was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures; the comparison distinguishes the communal promise from the named resurrection.
source_text: He will restore us to health after two days; on the third day we will rise and live before Him.

target_units.text: For I handed over to you as matters of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures,
and that He was buried, and that He has been raised on the third day according to the Scriptures,

relationship: shared early-and-late rain language in renewed divine provision
rationale: Hosea compares God's coming to early and late rain as the people pursue knowledge of Him. Joel promises early and late rainfall to Zion's children; it describes rainfall itself rather than repeating Hosea's comparison of God to rain.
source_text: We will know; we will pursue knowledge of the Lord. We will find Him ready like dawn, and He will come to us like rain, early and late upon the land.”

target_units.text: Children of Zion, rejoice and be glad in the Lord your God, because He gave you food for righteousness, and He will rain upon you early and late rainfall as before.

relationship: internal recurrence of the vanishing cloud-and-dew image
rationale: Hosea first compares the people's mercy to a morning cloud and passing dew. The later judgment applies the same two images to the people themselves, changing the object of the comparison while retaining its transience.
source_text: What shall I do with you, Ephraim? What shall I do with you, Judah? Your mercy is like a morning cloud and like morning dew passing away.

target_units.text: Therefore they will be like a morning cloud and like morning dew passing away, like chaff blown from a threshing floor and like vapor from locusts.

relationship: related lethal force of divinely spoken words
rationale: Hosea says God killed the prophets with His mouth's words. Jeremiah depicts God's words in the prophet's mouth as fire consuming the people as wood; the recipients and the mouth through which the words act are distinct.
source_text: Therefore I mowed down your prophets; I killed them with the words of My mouth, and My judgment will go forth like light.

target_units.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Almighty: Because you spoke this utterance, behold, I have made My words fire in your mouth, and this people wood, and it will devour them.

relationship: explicit quotation concerning mercy toward sinners
rationale: Jesus quotes Hosea's preference for mercy over sacrifice when answering criticism of His eating with tax collectors and sinners. Matthew gives the mercy clause, while Hosea also expressly prefers knowledge of God to whole burnt offerings.
source_text: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice, and knowledge of God rather than whole burnt offerings.

target_units.text: Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice.’ For I did not come to call righteous people, but sinners.”

relationship: explicit quotation against condemning the guiltless
rationale: Jesus again uses Hosea's mercy-over-sacrifice words in the dispute over His disciples plucking grain on the Sabbath. This application specifically rebukes condemning the guiltless, a distinct setting from Matthew 9.
source_text: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice, and knowledge of God rather than whole burnt offerings.

target_units.text: If you had known what ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice’ means, you would not have condemned the guiltless.

relationship: related defilement of both sister communities
rationale: Hosea links Ephraim's prostitution with Israel and Judah being defiled. Ezekiel's two women, identified in the context as Samaria and Jerusalem, share a way of defilement, with Oholibah's corruption exceeding her sister's.
source_text: In Israel’s house I saw dreadful things, there Ephraim’s prostitution; Israel and Judah were defiled.

target_units.text: Her sister Oholibah saw this and corrupted her desire beyond hers, and her prostitution beyond her sister’s prostitution.
She set her desire upon Assyrians’ sons, leaders and generals near her, clothed in finely bordered garments, horsemen riding horses; all choice young men.
I saw that she was defiled; one way for the two.

relationship: related harvest language joined to reversal of captivity
rationale: Hosea commands harvesting when God turns back His people's captivity. The psalm asks for captivity to be turned back and describes sowers returning with sheaves and exultation.
source_text: Begin harvesting for yourself when I turn back My people’s captivity,

target_units.text: Turn back our captivity, Lord, like torrents in the south.
Those sowing in tears will reap with exultation.
Going, they went and wept, carrying their seeds; but coming, they will arrive with exultation, carrying their sheaves.

relationship: specific roadside stripping by robbers
rationale: Hosea includes a robber stripping someone on his road in the exposure of injustice. Jesus' parable describes robbers stripping a traveler on the Jerusalem-Jericho road; the comparison concerns the concrete assault, without equating the two settings.
source_text: when I heal Israel. Ephraim’s injustice and Samaria’s wickedness will be uncovered, because they practiced falsehood. A thief will enter upon him, a robber stripping him on his road,

target_units.text: Jesus replied, “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers. They stripped him, inflicted blows, and went away, leaving him half dead.

relationship: close placement of wrongs before God's face
rationale: Hosea says God remembered their evils and that their schemes came before His face. The psalm likewise says their lawless deeds were set before God and their age is in His face's light.
source_text: so that they sing together as people singing together with their heart. I remembered all their evils; now their schemes have surrounded them; they have come before My face.

target_units.text: Thou didst set our lawless deeds before Thee; our age is in the light of Thy face.

relationship: related royal receptiveness to wrongdoing
rationale: Hosea charges that evils gladdened kings and falsehoods gladdened rulers. Proverbs describes a king listening to an unjust word and lawlessness among those under him; both connect corrupt speech and conduct with the royal setting.
source_text: With their evils they gladdened kings, and with their falsehoods, rulers.

target_units.text: When a king listens to an unjust word, all those under him are lawless.

relationship: parallel collective adultery expressed through vivid appetite imagery
rationale: Hosea calls all of them adulterers and compares them to a burning oven. Jeremiah likewise describes adultery and prostitutes' houses, comparing the men to horses longing for their neighbors' wives; the figurative vehicles differ.
source_text: All are adulterers, like an oven burning for the baking of something scorched by flame, from the kneading of fat until it ferments.

target_units.text: For which of these things should I be merciful to you? Your sons abandoned Me and swore by those who are not gods. And I fed them fully, and they committed adultery and lodged in prostitutes’ houses.
They became horses mad for mares; each neighed after his neighbor’s wife.

relationship: parallel disorder among leaders associated with wine
rationale: Hosea describes rulers raging from wine on the kings' days. Isaiah describes priest and prophet losing their senses and reeling through wine and sikera; the affected offices and particular actions differ.
source_text: On your kings’ days the rulers began to rage from wine; he stretched out his hand with pestilent men,

target_units.text: For these have been led astray by wine and wandered because of sikera. Priest and prophet lost their senses because of wine, reeled from sikera’s intoxication and went astray. This is an apparition.

relationship: same-chapter development of the heated oven image
rationale: The earlier verse depicts the adulterers as a burning oven. This verse returns to the oven image for their kindled hearts while they batter people, adding overnight sleep and morning blaze to the comparison.
source_text: because their hearts were kindled like an oven as they battered people. All night Ephraim was filled with sleep; morning came, and he was kindled like fire’s blaze.

target_units.text: All are adulterers, like an oven burning for the baking of something scorched by flame, from the kneading of fat until it ferments.

relationship: parallel failure to recognize destructive losses
rationale: Hosea says foreigners consumed Ephraim's strength without his recognizing it. Isaiah describes Israel being plundered and overpowered by war and burning without understanding or taking it to soul.
source_text: Foreigners devoured his strength, but he did not recognize it; gray hairs blossomed upon him, but he did not know it.

target_units.text: Who gave Jacob over to plunder and Israel to those despoiling him? Was it not God, against whom they sinned, refusing to walk in His ways or listen to His law?
He brought His wrathful anger upon them; war overpowered them, as did those burning them all around. None of them understood, nor did they take it to soul.

relationship: close refusal to return despite affliction
rationale: Hosea says Israel did not return to God or seek Him amid these things. Amos repeatedly describes blows and devastation followed by the charge that even so the people did not turn to Him.
source_text: Israel’s arrogance will be humbled before his face, yet they did not return to the Lord their God or seek Him in all these things.

target_units.text: “I struck you with burning and jaundice. You multiplied your gardens; the caterpillar devoured your vineyards, fig orchards and olive groves, yet not even so did you turn to Me,” says the Lord.

“I sent death among you on Egypt’s road and killed your young men with the sword, along with the captivity of your horses. I brought your camps up in fire in My anger; yet not even so did you turn to Me,” says the Lord.
“I overthrew you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you became like a firebrand snatched from fire. Yet not even so did you turn to Me,” says the Lord.

relationship: related unwise appeal to Egypt for help
rationale: Hosea depicts Ephraim as a senseless dove calling on Egypt and going to the Assyrians. Isaiah condemns going to Egypt without asking God and says Pharaoh's shelter becomes shame; the Egyptian appeal is shared, while Hosea also names Assyria.
source_text: Ephraim was like a senseless dove without understanding; he called on Egypt, and they went to the Assyrians.

target_units.text: “Woe, rebellious children,” thus says the Lord, “you made a plan not through Me and agreements not through My spirit, to add sins upon sins,
you who go down to Egypt, but they did not ask Me, to be helped by Pharaoh and sheltered by Egyptians.
For Pharaoh’s shelter will become your shame, and reproach for those trusting in Egypt.

relationship: close divine net spread over those facing judgment
rationale: Hosea says God will cast His net over them and bring them down like birds. Ezekiel likewise promises God's net over the ruler and captivity in Babylon; the recipients and accompanying images differ.
source_text: Whenever they go, I will cast My net over them; I will bring them down like heaven’s birds. I will discipline them when their affliction is heard.

target_units.text: I will spread My net over him, and he will be caught in My enclosure. I will bring him to Babylon, to the Chaldeans’ land, and he will not see it, and there he will die.

relationship: parallel accusation of speaking falsely against the Lord
rationale: Hosea contrasts God's redemption with their falsehoods against Him. Jeremiah likewise says they lied to their own Lord and denied that sword or famine would come; it specifies the false speech differently.
source_text: Woe to them, because they sprang away from Me! They are miserable, because they acted impiously toward Me. I redeemed them, but they spoke falsehoods against Me.

target_units.text: They lied to their own Lord and said: These things are not so; evils will not come upon us, and we will not see sword or famine.

relationship: related self-cutting within failed religious appeals
rationale: Hosea contrasts lack of heartfelt crying to God with howling and cutting themselves over grain and wine. Kings depicts Baal's prophets calling and cutting themselves without an answering voice; Hosea does not identify its participants as that particular group.
source_text: Their hearts did not cry to Me; they only howled on their beds. They cut themselves over grain and wine. They were disciplined through Me,

target_units.text: They took the young bull and prepared it. They called on Baal’s name from morning until noon, saying, “Hear us, Baal, hear us!” But there was no voice and no hearing. They ran about on the altar they had made.
At noon Elijah the Tishbite mocked them and said, “Call with a loud voice, for he is a god! He has chattering to do; perhaps he is also conducting business, or perhaps he is asleep and will get up!”
They called with a loud voice and cut themselves according to their custom with knives and lances, until blood poured over them.

relationship: shared turning-away and bow imagery with different descriptions
rationale: Hosea says they turned toward nothing and became like a drawn bow. The psalm joins turning back and breaking faith with becoming a crooked bow; its crooked description must not replace Hosea's drawn bow.
source_text: They turned away toward nothing; they became like a drawn bow. Their rulers will fall by the sword because of their tongues’ lack of discipline. This is their contempt in Egypt’s land.

target_units.text: and turned back and broke faith just like their fathers, and changed into a crooked bow,

relationship: related eagle image for threatening approach
rationale: Hosea places an eagle against the Lord's house in an accusation of covenant and law transgression. Deuteronomy warns of a distant nation coming like an eagle's swoop; the comparison does not resolve Hosea's unusual opening bosom-and-earth phrase.
source_text: Into their bosom like earth, like an eagle against the Lord’s house, because they transgressed My covenant and acted impiously against My law.

target_units.text: The Lord shall bring against you a nation from afar, from the end of the earth, as the swooping of an eagle, a nation whose speech you shall not understand,

relationship: related claimed relationship accompanied by rejected lawlessness
rationale: Hosea gives the cry, God, we know Thee, within the covenant-breaking accusation. Matthew contrasts calling Lord, Lord with the rejection of those practicing lawlessness and the declaration I never knew you; the direction of the knowing claim differs.
source_text: They will cry to Me, ‘God, we know Thee!’

target_units.text: Not everyone who says to Me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of the heavens, but the one who does the will of My Father in the heavens.
Many will say to Me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in Thy name, cast out demons in Thy name, and do many mighty works in Thy name?’
Then I will declare to them, ‘I never knew you. Depart from Me, you who practice lawlessness.’

relationship: concrete parallel of precious metal fashioned into an idol
rationale: Hosea charges that the people made silver and gold into idols. Exodus narrates gold earrings received by Aaron and fashioned into a cast calf; it supplies a concrete instance without identifying it as Hosea's later calf.
source_text: They reigned for themselves and not through Me; they ruled and did not make it known to Me. They made their silver and gold into idols for themselves, so that they might be destroyed.

target_units.text: Aaron said to them, “Take off the gold earrings from the ears of your wives and daughters, and bring them to me.”
All the people took off the gold earrings from their ears and brought them to Aaron.
He received them from their hands, fashioned them with an engraving tool, and made them into a cast calf. He said, “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you up from the land of Egypt.”

relationship: related angry rejection of a calf image
rationale: Hosea commands Samaria to rub away its calf and declares God's provoked anger. Exodus records Moses' anger and destruction of the calf; the commands, agents and procedures are distinct.
source_text: Rub away your calf, Samaria! My anger was provoked against them. How long will they be incapable of being cleansed

target_units.text: As he approached the camp, he saw the calf and the dancing. In his anger Moses threw the two tablets from his hands and shattered them at the mountain’s foot.
He took the calf they had made, burned it in the fire, ground it fine, scattered it on the water, and made the sons of Israel drink it.

relationship: parallel rejection of human-made objects as divine powers
rationale: Hosea says a craftsman made the calf and it is no god. Jeremiah describes carpentry and metal decoration producing objects that must be carried and cannot provide good; both expose the dependence of the worshipped objects on makers.
source_text: in Israel? A craftsman made it, and it is no god, because your calf was leading people astray, Samaria.

target_units.text: For the nations’ customs are futile: it is wood cut from the woodland, a carpenter’s work and a cast object.
They are adorned with silver and gold; with hammers and nails they fastened them, and they will not move.
They must be lifted and carried, because they will not take a step. Do not fear them, because they certainly will not do evil, and no good is in them.

relationship: close threat of foreigners consuming the harvest
rationale: Hosea says even flour from the weak sheaf will be consumed by foreigners. Deuteronomy likewise threatens an unknown nation consuming the land's yield and all the people's labor; Hosea's opening wind-blasted sowing is not recast as a whirlwind.
source_text: Because they sowed wind-blasted things, their overthrow will receive them: a sheaf without strength to make flour. Even if it does make flour, foreigners will devour it.

target_units.text: A nation which you do not know shall consume the yield of your land and all your labours; and you shall be wronged and crushed all your days.

relationship: close useless-vessel image for rejection and displacement
rationale: Hosea depicts Israel among the nations as a useless vessel. Jeremiah describes Jeconiah as a vessel of no use, cast into an unknown land; the collective people and named individual remain distinct.
source_text: Israel was swallowed up; now he became among the nations like a useless vessel.

target_units.text: Jeconiah was dishonored like a vessel for which there is no use, because he was cast out and thrown into a land he did not know.

relationship: internal recurrence of Assyrian diplomacy
rationale: Hosea first describes going to the Assyrians and loving gifts. The later accusation explicitly names an Assyrian covenant and trade with Egypt; it develops the recurring foreign-relations theme without turning Ephraim's flourishing into a wild-ass image.
source_text: Because they went up to the Assyrians; Ephraim flourished by himself, and they loved gifts.

target_units.text: But Ephraim is an evil spirit; he pursued scorching heat all day, multiplied empty and worthless things, made a covenant with the Assyrians, and traded oil into Egypt.

relationship: parallel multiplication of altars within condemned worship
rationale: Hosea says multiplying altars produced occasions of sin for Ephraim. Jeremiah describes altars for Baal corresponding to Jerusalem's exits and gods as numerous as Judah's cities, another accusation of proliferating worship sites.
source_text: Because Ephraim multiplied altars, beloved altars became occasions of sin for him.

target_units.text: For your gods were according to the number of your cities, Judah; and according to the number of Jerusalem’s exits you set up altars to burn incense to Baal.

relationship: close rejection of sacrifice amid disobedience
rationale: Hosea says sacrifices and meat will not secure God's acceptance and announces remembrance of sins. Jeremiah likewise rejects whole burnt offerings and sacrifices after charging rejection of God's word and law.
source_text: Because even if they offer a sacrifice and eat meat, the Lord will not accept them. Now He will remember their injustices and punish their sins. They returned to Egypt and will eat unclean things among the Assyrians.

target_units.text: Hear, earth! Behold, I am bringing evils upon this people, the fruit of their turning away, because they did not attend to My words and rejected My law.
Why do you bring Me frankincense from Sheba and cinnamon from a distant land? Your whole burnt offerings are not acceptable, and your sacrifices did not please Me.

relationship: close announced fire devouring urban foundations
rationale: Hosea mentions Judah's multiplied walled cities and announces fire devouring foundations. Amos likewise announces fire upon Judah that will devour Jerusalem's foundations, after charging rejection of God's law.
source_text: Israel forgot his Maker, and they built sacred precincts; Judah multiplied walled cities. I will send fire into his cities, and it will devour their foundations.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: “For three impieties of the sons of Judah, and for four, I will not turn away from him, because they rejected the Lord’s law and did not keep His ordinances. Their vain things, which they made, led them astray—the things their fathers followed.
I will send fire upon Judah, and it will devour Jerusalem’s foundations.”

relationship: internal relation between prostitution imagery and desired provision
rationale: Hosea condemns loving gifts at grain threshing floors while prostituting oneself away from God. The earlier woman likewise says she will follow lovers whom she credits with bread and other necessities; both join unfaithfulness with desired material provision.
source_text: Do not rejoice, Israel, or be glad like the peoples, because you prostituted yourself away from your God; you loved gifts on every threshing floor of grain.

target_units.text: For their mother prostituted herself; she who bore them brought shame. She said, ‘I will follow my lovers, who give me my loaves and water, my garments and linen cloths, my oil and everything due to me.’

relationship: close prediction of eating unclean things among foreign peoples
rationale: Hosea names eating unclean things among the Assyrians. Ezekiel's food-sign instruction likewise announces that Israel's sons will eat unclean things among the nations, without naming Assyria in that unit.
source_text: They did not dwell in the Lord’s land; Ephraim dwelt in Egypt, and among the Assyrians they will eat unclean things.

target_units.text: and say, ‘Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: So the sons of Israel will eat unclean things among the nations.’”

relationship: related mourning, food and ritual uncleanness
rationale: Hosea compares the sacrifices to defiling bread of mourning, excluded from the Lord's house. Deuteronomy's tithe declaration expressly denies eating the holy produce in mourning or offering it for an unclean use; the legal and judgment settings differ.
source_text: They did not pour wine to the Lord or make it pleasant to Him. Their sacrifices are like bread of mourning to them; all who eat them will be defiled, because their loaves for their own lives will not enter the Lord’s house.

target_units.text: And I have not eaten thereof in my mourning, neither have I offered thereof for an unclean use, nor given thereof unto the dead. I have hearkened unto the voice of the Lord my God; I have done according to all that Thou hast commanded me.

relationship: parallel thorns in human habitations under judgment
rationale: Hosea's announcement of departure and burial includes thorns in the people's dwellings. Isaiah likewise describes thorny trees sprouting in cities and fortifications; the named places and other judgments differ.
source_text: Therefore look, they will go away from Egypt’s misery; Memphis will receive them, and Machmas will bury them. Destruction will inherit their silver; thorns will be in their dwellings.

target_units.text: Thorny trees will sprout in their cities and her fortifications; she will become a dwelling for sirens and a courtyard for ostriches.

relationship: close phrase days of vengeance in announced calamity
rationale: Hosea announces that the days of vengeance and repayment have come. Luke calls the impending days around Jerusalem days of vengeance for what is written to be fulfilled; this is a verbal and judgment-setting comparison, not an equation of the events.
source_text: The days of vengeance have come; the days of your repayment have come. Israel will be afflicted like the deranged prophet, a spirit-bearing man. Because your injustices were many, your madness increased.

target_units.text: because these are days of vengeance, for all that is written to be fulfilled.

relationship: related prophetic watchman language with contrasting duties and danger
rationale: Hosea places Ephraim's watchman with God and then describes a prophet as a crooked trap. Ezekiel appoints the son of man as Israel's watchman to convey God's warning; the comparison preserves Hosea's distinct clauses rather than merging their figures.
source_text: Ephraim’s watchman is with God; a prophet, a crooked trap upon all his ways. They fixed madness in the Lord’s house.

target_units.text: “Son of man, I have appointed you a watchman for the house of Israel. You will hear a word from My mouth and convey My warning to them.

relationship: internal repeated announcement of remembering and punishing sins
rationale: Both passages announce God's remembrance of injustices and punishment of sins. Hosea 9 adds corruption as in the hill's days; this comparison does not assign that unnamed reference to a particular historical incident.
source_text: They were corrupted as in the hill’s days. He will remember his injustices; He will punish his sins.

target_units.text: Because even if they offer a sacrifice and eat meat, the Lord will not accept them. Now He will remember their injustices and punish their sins. They returned to Egypt and will eat unclean things among the Assyrians.

relationship: related account of Israel's attachment to the Peor cult
rationale: Hosea recalls Israel's going to Beel-phegor and becoming estranged into shame. Numbers narrates Israel's participation in sacrifices and initiation into worship called Baal of Peor; the native forms of the cult name are preserved.
source_text: Like a cluster of grapes in a wilderness I found Israel, and like an early lookout in a fig tree I saw their fathers. They went to Beel-phegor and became estranged into shame, and the beloved became like the detested.

target_units.text: And Israel lodged at Shittim, and the people profaned themselves by engaging in sexual immorality with the daughters of Moab.
And they invited them to the sacrifices of their idols. The people ate from their sacrifices and bowed down to their idols.
And Israel was initiated into the worship of Baal of Peor, and the Lord became angry with Israel.

relationship: related threatened loss of children
rationale: Hosea says that even rearing children will end in bereavement. Deuteronomy describes sons and daughters given to another nation while their parents watch helplessly; these are distinct forms of parental loss, without explaining Hosea's separate My-flesh clause.
source_text: because even if they rear their children, they will be bereaved among humankind. Indeed, woe is upon them: My flesh is from them.

target_units.text: Your sons and your daughters shall be given unto another nation, and your eyes shall look upon them and waste away; and your hand shall have no strength.

relationship: close barren-womb and unnourishing-breast language under calamity
rationale: Hosea asks for a childless womb and dry breasts. Jesus predicts days when people will call the barren, wombs that did not bear and breasts that did not nourish blessed; the request and future saying differ within their respective judgment settings.
source_text: Give them, Lord—what wilt Thou give them? Give them a childless womb and dry breasts.

target_units.text: For behold, days are coming in which they will say, ‘Blessed are the barren, and the wombs that did not bear, and the breasts that did not nourish.’

relationship: related divine rejection of house and inheritance
rationale: Hosea announces hatred at Gilgal, expulsion from God's house and an end to love. Jeremiah likewise speaks of abandoning God's house and hating the inheritance that raised its voice against Him; the descriptions of rejection differ.
source_text: All their evils are at Gilgal, because there I hated them. Because of their wicked practices I will expel them from My house. I will certainly love them no longer; all their rulers are disobedient.
