target_units.text: I have abandoned My house, let go My inheritance, and given My beloved soul into her enemies’ hands.
My inheritance became to Me like a lion in woodland; she raised her voice against Me, therefore I hated her.

relationship: close dried-root image for destructive judgment
rationale: Hosea describes Ephraim dried at the roots and unable to bear fruit. Bildad likewise describes roots drying below and harvest falling above; the shared plant image does not make his depicted individual identical with Ephraim.
source_text: Ephraim suffered; he dried up at his roots; he will certainly bear fruit no longer. Even if they give birth, I will kill the desired offspring of their womb.

target_units.text: Below, his roots will dry up; above, his harvest will fall.

relationship: parallel displacement among nations without settled rest
rationale: Hosea predicts rejection for not listening and wandering among the nations. Deuteronomy likewise describes scattering among all nations and no resting place for the foot within its warnings for disobedience.
source_text: God will thrust them away because they did not listen to Him, and they will be wanderers among the nations.

target_units.text: And the Lord your God shall scatter you among all the nations, from one end of the earth unto the other; and there you shall serve other gods, wood and stone, which neither you nor your fathers have known.

And among those nations He shall give you no rest, neither shall there be a resting place for the sole of your foot; and the Lord shall give you there a faint heart, and failing eyes, and a wasting soul.

relationship: parallel identification of Israel through vine or vineyard imagery
rationale: Hosea portrays Israel as a luxuriant, fruitful vine whose abundance accompanies multiplied altars. Isaiah identifies the Lord's vineyard as Israel's house and contrasts expected judgment with lawlessness; Hosea's thriving fruit is not changed into Isaiah's failed moral yield.
source_text: Israel is a vine with luxuriant branches, its fruit thriving. According to the abundance of his fruits he multiplied altars; according to his land’s good things he built pillars.

target_units.text: For the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is Israel’s house, and the man of Judah a beloved new planting. I waited for it to produce judgment, but it produced lawlessness, not righteousness but an outcry.

relationship: related challenge to divided religious allegiance
rationale: Hosea says they divided their hearts and announces destruction of altars and pillars. Elijah asks how long the people will limp on both knees and sets following the Lord against following Baal; the heart and knee images differ.
source_text: They divided their hearts; now they will disappear. He will demolish their altars, and their pillars will suffer devastation.

target_units.text: Elijah came near them all and said to them, “How long will you limp on both your knees? If the Lord is God, follow Him; if Baal is, follow him.” The people did not answer a word.

relationship: related questioning of reliance on rulers
rationale: Hosea's people ask what a king can do for them after failing to fear the Lord. The psalm warns against trust in rulers who have no salvation and instead commends hope in the Lord.
source_text: Because now they will say, ‘We have no king, because we did not fear the Lord; and the king—what will he do for us?’

target_units.text: Do not trust in rulers and in sons of men who have no salvation.
His spirit will go out, and he will return to his earth; on that day all their reasonings will perish.
Happy the one whose Helper is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the Lord his God,

relationship: related bound cult images carried away
rationale: Hosea describes the object bound and carried to the Assyrians as a gift for King Jarim. Isaiah likewise describes named carved images bound as burdens and led captive; the names, destinations and gift setting are not equated.
source_text: They bound it and carried it to the Assyrians as guest-gifts for King Jarim. He will receive Ephraim as a gift, and Israel will be ashamed of his counsel.

target_units.text: Bel fell; Dagon was shattered. Their carved images became a burden for wild and domestic animals. Lift them, bound together, as a load for one who is weary
and hungry and exhausted, without strength at all; they cannot be saved from war, and they themselves were led captive.

relationship: close mountain-and-hill appeal with the commands reversed
rationale: Hosea gives the appeals to mountains to cover and hills to fall upon the people. Jesus predicts appeals to mountains to fall and hills to cover; the distinctive paired appeals correspond while the assigned commands are reversed.
source_text: The shrines of On, Israel’s sins, will be removed; thorns and thistles will grow on their altars. They will say to the mountains, ‘Cover us!’ and to the hills, ‘Fall upon us!’

target_units.text: Then they will begin to say to the mountains, ‘Fall upon us,’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us.’

relationship: related calf imagery for Ephraim with different training descriptions
rationale: Hosea calls Ephraim a heifer trained to love strife. Jeremiah's Ephraim describes himself as a calf not taught and speaks of God's discipline; the contrast preserves strife rather than substituting threshing for Hosea's wording.
source_text: Ephraim is a heifer trained to love strife, but I will come upon the finest part of her neck. I will mount Ephraim and pass over Judah in silence; Jacob will strengthen him.

target_units.text: I surely heard Ephraim wailing: Thou didst discipline me, and I was disciplined; like a calf I was not taught. Turn me back, and I will return, because Thou art the Lord my God.

relationship: close moral sowing and reaping of life
rationale: Hosea commands sowing in righteousness and reaping life's fruit. Galatians describes sowing into the Spirit and reaping eternal life, encouraging perseverance in good; the descriptions of the sowing are distinct.
source_text: Sow for yourselves in righteousness; reap life’s fruit. Shine a light of knowledge for yourselves; seek the Lord until produce of righteousness comes to you.

target_units.text: For the one who sows into his own flesh will reap corruption from the flesh, but the one who sows into the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit.
And let us not grow weary in doing good, for in the proper season we will reap, if we do not give up.

relationship: shared sowing and fruit-of-righteousness imagery
rationale: Hosea links righteous sowing and the arrival of produce of righteousness with seeking God. James describes a fruit of righteousness sown in peace for peacemakers, adding a particular peace-making setting to the cultivation image.
source_text: Sow for yourselves in righteousness; reap life’s fruit. Shine a light of knowledge for yourselves; seek the Lord until produce of righteousness comes to you.

target_units.text: And a fruit of righteousness is sown in peace for those who make peace.

relationship: related eating of the consequences of one's wrong way
rationale: Hosea describes reaping injustices and eating false fruit amid reliance on chariots and force. Wisdom in Proverbs says the rejecters of her counsel will eat their own way's fruits and be filled with their ungodliness.
source_text: Why did you pass over impiety in silence and reap its injustices, eating false fruit? Because you hoped in your chariots, in the multitude of your force.

target_units.text: Therefore they will eat the fruits of their own way and be filled with their own ungodliness.

relationship: related wartime violence against mothers and children
rationale: Hosea describes a mother dashed upon children in days of war. Elisha predicts Hazael's burning of strongholds, dashing of infants and tearing of pregnant women; the atrocities are compared without identifying Hazael with Hosea's Salaman.
source_text: Destruction will arise among your people, and all your walled places will vanish. As the ruler Salaman from the house of Jerobaal, in days of war they dashed a mother to the ground upon children.

target_units.text: Hazael said, ‘Why does my lord weep?’ He said, ‘Because I know all the evils you will do to the sons of Israel: you will send their strongholds into fire, kill their chosen men with the sword, dash down their infants, and tear open their pregnant women.’

relationship: internal recurrence of judgment against Israel's royal rule
rationale: Hosea's opening announces an end to the kingdom of Israel's house. The later declaration says Israel's king was cast off because of the people's evils; it does not name that king or equate the announcements' precise timing.
source_text: So I will do to you, house of Israel, because of your evils. At dawn they were cast off; Israel’s king was cast off.

target_units.text: The Lord said to him, “Call him Jezreel, for in a little while I will avenge Jezreel’s blood upon Jehu’s house and put an end to the kingdom of Israel’s house.

relationship: explicit fulfillment citation with a changed filial formulation
rationale: Matthew applies an Egypt saying to the Child's stay there and quotes My Son. The supplied Hosea text instead says God loved infant Israel and summoned his children from Egypt; the plural and possessive difference is preserved.
source_text: Because Israel was an infant, I loved him, and out of Egypt I summoned his children.

target_units.text: He remained there until Herod’s death, so that what was spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled: “Out of Egypt I called My Son.”

relationship: parallel divine approach answered by disobedience and illicit worship
rationale: Hosea contrasts God's summoning with departure, Baal sacrifices and incense to images. Isaiah describes God's outstretched hands to a disobedient people who provoke Him with sacrifices and incense; the described worship sites differ.
source_text: As I summoned them, so they departed from My presence; they sacrificed to the Baalim and burned incense to carved images.

target_units.text: I spread out My hands all day to a disobedient, contradicting people who did not walk in a true way but followed their sins.
This people continually provokes Me to My face. They sacrifice in gardens and burn incense on bricks to demons that do not exist,

relationship: related divine carrying and care from early life
rationale: Hosea says God bound Ephraim's feet, took him upon His arm and healed without being recognized. Isaiah addresses Israel as carried from the belly and promises to take them up and save them; Hosea's binding is not rewritten as teaching to walk.
source_text: I bound Ephraim’s feet together; I took him up on My arm, but they did not know that I have healed them.

target_units.text: “Listen to Me, house of Jacob and all Israel’s remnant, you who are carried from the belly and instructed from childhood.
Until old age I am, and until you grow very old I am. I bear with you; I made you, and I will release you. I will take you up and save you.

relationship: internal pairing of Egypt and Assyria in Ephraim's condition
rationale: Both passages state that Ephraim dwelt in Egypt and also speak of Assyria. The earlier passage adds unclean eating among Assyrians; the later calls Assur his king and names refusal to return, without specifying one shared historical episode.
source_text: Ephraim dwelt in Egypt, and Assur himself was his king, because he did not wish to return.

target_units.text: They did not dwell in the Lord’s land; Ephraim dwelt in Egypt, and among the Assyrians they will eat unclean things.

relationship: related eating from one's own wrongful course
rationale: Hosea says they will eat from their schemes. Wisdom's warning says her rejecters will eat the fruits of their own way; the comparison concerns that consequence image and does not resolve Hosea's preceding weakened-sword clauses.
source_text: A sword grew weak in his cities and ceased in his hands, and they will eat from their schemes.

target_units.text: Therefore they will eat the fruits of their own way and be filled with their own ungodliness.

relationship: named city-overthrow precedent contrasted with hesitation to destroy
rationale: Hosea asks about making Israel like Adama and Seboim and describes God's stirred change of mind. Deuteronomy names Admah and Zeboiim among cities the Lord overthrew in anger; the native name forms and the contrasting responses are preserved.
source_text: How shall I deal with you, Ephraim? Shall I shield you, Israel? How shall I deal with you? Shall I make you like Adama and like Seboim? My heart turned within itself; My change of mind was stirred together.

target_units.text: sulfur and salt, burned over; all its land shall neither be sown nor sprout, neither shall any green thing grow upon it, as at the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, which the Lord overthrew in wrath and anger—

relationship: close assertion that God is not a human being
rationale: Hosea grounds the refusal to erase Ephraim in God's being God rather than human. Numbers likewise says God is not as a human to be led astray or threatened and asks whether His speech will be fulfilled; its particular predicates differ.
source_text: I will certainly not act according to My furious anger; I will certainly not abandon Ephraim to be erased. For I am God and not a human being, holy within you, and I will not enter a city.

target_units.text: God is not as a man, to be led astray, nor as a son of man, to be threatened; having spoken, shall He not act? Shall He speak, and not abide by it?

relationship: related roaring-lion imagery joined to response to God
rationale: Hosea says the Lord will roar like a lion and describes children of waters being astonished. Amos pairs a lion's roar and fear with the Lord's speech and prophecy; it does not directly repeat Hosea's description of the Lord roaring.
source_text: I will walk after the Lord. He will roar like a lion, because He Himself will howl, and children of waters will be astonished.

target_units.text: A lion will roar—and who will not fear? The Lord God has spoken—and who will not prophesy?

relationship: close restoration from both Egypt and Assyria
rationale: Hosea compares those from Egypt and Assyria to birds and promises restored houses. Isaiah likewise gathers those lost in Assyria and Egypt to worship the Lord in Jerusalem; its trumpet and destination differ from Hosea's details.
source_text: They will be astonished like a bird from Egypt and like a dove from the Assyrians’ land, and I will restore them to their houses, says the Lord.

target_units.text: On that day they will sound the great trumpet. Those lost in the Assyrians’ country and those lost in Egypt will come and bow to the Lord upon the holy mountain in Jerusalem.

relationship: parallel accusation of Israel and Judah's rejection and falsehood
rationale: Hosea names Ephraim's falsehood and impieties involving Israel's house and Judah. Jeremiah likewise charges both houses with rejection and lying to their Lord; the comparison concerns these accusations, not Hosea's subsequent holy-people naming.
source_text: Ephraim surrounded Me with falsehood, and Israel’s house and Judah with impieties. Now God knew them, and he will be called God’s holy people.

target_units.text: For the house of Israel and the house of Judah have utterly rejected Me, says the Lord.
They lied to their own Lord and said: These things are not so; evils will not come upon us, and we will not see sword or famine.

relationship: related foreign agreements involving Egypt without fidelity to God
rationale: Hosea condemns an Assyrian covenant and oil trade into Egypt. Isaiah condemns agreements made without God's spirit and going to Egypt without asking Him; the specific partners and transactions remain different.
source_text: But Ephraim is an evil spirit; he pursued scorching heat all day, multiplied empty and worthless things, made a covenant with the Assyrians, and traded oil into Egypt.

target_units.text: “Woe, rebellious children,” thus says the Lord, “you made a plan not through Me and agreements not through My spirit, to add sins upon sins,
you who go down to Egypt, but they did not ask Me, to be helped by Pharaoh and sheltered by Egyptians.
For Pharaoh’s shelter will become your shame, and reproach for those trusting in Egypt.

relationship: close divine repayment according to ways and practices
rationale: Hosea announces repayment to Jacob according to his ways and practices. Jeremiah likewise describes the Lord giving each person according to ways and the fruits of practices, after examining hearts and kidneys.
source_text: The Lord has a case against Judah, to exact punishment on Jacob according to his ways; He will repay him according to his practices.

target_units.text: I, the Lord, examine hearts and test kidneys, to give each according to his ways and the fruits of his practices.

relationship: related account of Jacob and his brother at birth
rationale: Hosea says he tripped his brother in the womb. Genesis narrates Jacob emerging with his hand holding Esau's heel; the connection preserves the differing location and action instead of treating the wording as identical.
source_text: In the womb he tripped up his brother, and in his labors he prevailed against God

target_units.text: And her days to give birth were fulfilled, and behold, there were twins in her womb.
And the firstborn son came out red, all over like a hairy hide; and he was named Esau.
And afterward his brother came out, and his hand held Esau’s heel; and he was named Jacob. And Isaac was sixty years old when Rebekah bore them.

relationship: narrative counterpart to Jacob's prevailing with God
rationale: Hosea recalls Jacob prevailing against God in his labors. Genesis narrates his wrestling and the declaration that he has been strong with God and mighty with men; this is distinct from the source's earlier womb episode.
source_text: In the womb he tripped up his brother, and in his labors he prevailed against God

target_units.text: And Jacob was left alone; and a man wrestled with him until morning.
And he saw that he could not prevail against him, and touched the broad part of his thigh; and the broad part of Jacob’s thigh became numb as he wrestled with him.
And he said to him, “Let me go, for dawn has risen.” And he said, “I will not let you go unless you bless me.”
And he said to him, “What is your name?” And he said, “Jacob.”
And he said to him, “Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name, for you have been strong with God, and with men you are mighty.”

relationship: related wrestling tradition with distinct descriptions of the counterpart
rationale: Hosea says he prevailed with an angel and was able. Genesis narrates wrestling with a man and being strong with God; the connection does not assign Hosea's subsequent plural weeping or house-of-On clauses wholly to Jacob.
source_text: and prevailed with an angel and was able. They wept and entreated Me; in the house of On they found Me, and there he was spoken to.

target_units.text: And Jacob was left alone; and a man wrestled with him until morning.
And he saw that he could not prevail against him, and touched the broad part of his thigh; and the broad part of Jacob’s thigh became numb as he wrestled with him.
And he said to him, “Let me go, for dawn has risen.” And he said, “I will not let you go unless you bless me.”
And he said to him, “What is your name?” And he said, “Jacob.”
And he said to him, “Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name, for you have been strong with God, and with men you are mighty.”
And Jacob asked and said, “Tell me your name.” And he said, “Why do you ask my name?” And he blessed him there.

relationship: close Lord-name and memorial language
rationale: Hosea names the Lord God Almighty as his memorial. Exodus likewise joins the Lord, God of the ancestors, with His everlasting name and memorial from generation to generation; the possessive formulations remain distinct.
source_text: The Lord God Almighty will be his memorial.

target_units.text: And God said again to Moses, “This is what you shall say to the sons of Israel: ‘The Lord, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.’ This is My everlasting name, and My memorial from generation to generation.

relationship: close pairing of mercy, judgment and approach to God
rationale: Hosea commands keeping mercy and judgment and drawing near to God continually. Micah's question names doing justice, loving mercy and readiness to walk with God as what the Lord seeks.
source_text: You will return in your God; keep mercy and judgment, and draw near to your God continually.

target_units.text: Has it been declared to you, O man, what is good? Or what does the Lord seek from you, except to do justice, and to love mercy, and to be ready to walk with the Lord your God?

relationship: specific condemnation of unjust scales
rationale: Hosea places a balance of injustice in Canaan's hand and charges love of domination. Proverbs likewise condemns deceitful scales and contrasts an acceptable just weight; the source's Canaan designation is retained.
source_text: Canaan—in his hand is a balance of injustice; he loved to dominate.

target_units.text: Deceitful scales are an abomination before the Lord, but a just weight is acceptable to Him.

relationship: related insecure self-satisfaction in riches
rationale: Ephraim claims riches and refreshment, but his labors will not be found for him because of his injustices. Luke's rich man likewise anticipates rest from stored goods but faces the demand for his soul and the question of who will possess them.
source_text: Ephraim said, ‘Indeed I have become rich; I have found refreshment for myself.’ All his labors will not be found for him because of the injustices in which he sinned.

target_units.text: And I will say to my soul, “Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years. Rest, eat, drink, be glad!”’
But God said to him, ‘Fool, this very night they demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared—whose will they be?’
So it is with the one who stores up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.”

relationship: close connection of tents, festival observance and exodus
rationale: Hosea recalls the Lord bringing Israel from Egypt and promises settlement in tents as on a festival day. Leviticus commands festival residence in tents to remember Israel's tent dwelling after the exodus; Hosea does not expressly name that festival.
source_text: But I, the Lord your God, brought you up from Egypt’s land; I will still settle you in tents as on a festival day.

target_units.text: You shall dwell in tents seven days; every native in Israel shall dwell in tents,
so that your generations may see that I made the sons of Israel dwell in tents when I brought them out of the land of Egypt. I am the Lord your God.

relationship: parallel prophetic revelation through visions and represented forms
rationale: Hosea describes speaking to prophets, multiplied visions and representation through prophets. Numbers likewise describes revelation in visions and sleep, then distinguishes Moses' visible, mouth-to-mouth encounter; its distinction is not erased.
source_text: I will speak to prophets; I multiplied visions and was represented in likenesses through prophets.

target_units.text: And He said unto them: Hear My words: If there is a prophet among you unto the Lord, I will make Myself known unto him in a vision, and I will speak unto him in sleep.
Not so My servant Moses; he is faithful in all My house.
I will speak unto him mouth to mouth, in visible appearance, and not through riddles; and he saw the glory of the Lord. And why were you not afraid to speak against My servant Moses?

relationship: narrative counterpart to service and pastoral labor for a wife
rationale: Hosea recalls Jacob's service for a wife and keeping guard for a wife. Jacob's speech in Genesis recounts flock care, compensation for losses and serving fourteen years for two daughters and six among sheep; the durations and plural wives are Genesis's added details.
source_text: Jacob withdrew to Syria’s plain; Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he kept guard.

target_units.text: “These twenty years I have been with you; your sheep and your goats have not miscarried, and I have not eaten the rams of your flock.
“I brought you no animal taken by wild beasts; I myself paid for what was stolen by day and what was stolen by night.
“By day I was consumed by the heat, and by night by the frost; and sleep departed from my eyes.
“These twenty years I have been in your house; I served you fourteen years for your two daughters, and six years among your sheep; and you defrauded me of my wages of ten ewe lambs.

relationship: narrative counterpart to the prophet leading Israel from Egypt
rationale: Hosea says the Lord brought Israel from Egypt through a prophet. Exodus records God's commission to Moses to bring Israel from Egypt and the promise of divine presence; Deuteronomy 34:10–12 also expressly calls Moses a prophet.
source_text: Through a prophet the Lord brought Israel up from Egypt, and through a prophet he was preserved.

target_units.text: Come now, and I will send you to Pharaoh king of Egypt; and you shall bring My people, the sons of Israel, out of the land of Egypt.”
Moses said to God, “Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and bring the sons of Israel out of the land of Egypt?”
And God said to Moses, “I will be with you; and this shall be the sign to you that I send you: when you have brought My people out of Egypt, you shall serve God upon this mountain.”

relationship: close blood-upon-the-wrongdoer judgment language
rationale: Hosea announces Ephraim's blood poured upon him and repayment for reproach. Ezekiel likewise says the lawless son's blood will be upon him after listing his acts; the collective and individual subjects remain distinct.
source_text: Ephraim provoked anger and exasperation; his blood will be poured upon him, and the Lord will repay him for his reproach.

target_units.text: gave at interest and took increase—this one certainly will not live. He committed all this lawlessness; he will surely be put to death, and his blood will be upon him.

relationship: related association of Baal worship with death
rationale: Hosea says Ephraim assigned his received ordinances to Baal and died. Numbers describes Israel's initiation into Baal of Peor worship and commands the killing of participants; it does not identify this as the same particular event.
source_text: According to Ephraim’s word, he received ordinances in Israel, assigned them to Baal and died.

target_units.text: And Israel was initiated into the worship of Baal of Peor, and the Lord became angry with Israel.
And the Lord said unto Moses: Take all the leaders of the people and make a public example of them before the Lord in the sunlight, and the Lord's fierce anger will turn away from Israel.
And Moses said to Israel's tribes: Each of you shall kill his own kinsman who was initiated into the worship of Baal of Peor.

relationship: related human sacrifice within image worship
rationale: Hosea reports a demand to sacrifice human beings because calves ran out amid manufactured silver images. The psalm narrates sacrifices of sons and daughters to Canaan's images; the demand and the narrated acts are distinct.
source_text: He still continued to sin, and they made themselves a cast image from their silver according to the likeness of idols, works completed for them by craftsmen. They say, ‘Sacrifice human beings, for calves have run out!’

target_units.text: They sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons,
and shed innocent blood, the blood of their sons and daughters whom they sacrificed to Canaan’s carved images; the land was murdered with blood,

relationship: close wind-scattered chaff image for the judged
rationale: Hosea compares the idolaters to chaff blown from a threshing floor among other vanishing images. The psalm likewise compares the ungodly to chaff flung away by the wind.
source_text: Therefore they will be like a morning cloud and like morning dew passing away, like chaff blown from a threshing floor and like vapor from locusts.

target_units.text: Not so the ungodly, not so, but like chaff which the wind flings away from the face of the earth.

relationship: close exclusive divine identity and saving power
rationale: Hosea declares that Israel shall know no god except the Lord and that none saves apart from Him. Isaiah likewise excludes other gods and declares that apart from God no one saves.
source_text: But I am the Lord your God, who establishes heaven and creates earth, whose hands created all heaven’s host. I did not display them to you so that you should follow them. I brought you up from Egypt’s land; you shall know no god except Me, and there is none who saves apart from Me.

target_units.text: Become witnesses for Me—and I too am a witness, says the Lord God, and the servant whom I chose—so that you may know, believe, and understand that I am. Before Me no other god came to be, nor will there be one after Me.
I am God, and apart from Me there is no one who saves.

relationship: close warning about heaven's host joined to deliverance from Egypt
rationale: Hosea says God created heaven's host without displaying it for Israel to follow, then recalls deliverance from Egypt. Deuteronomy warns against worshipping the celestial bodies and likewise recalls God taking Israel out of Egypt.
source_text: But I am the Lord your God, who establishes heaven and creates earth, whose hands created all heaven’s host. I did not display them to you so that you should follow them. I brought you up from Egypt’s land; you shall know no god except Me, and there is none who saves apart from Me.

target_units.text: And lest you lift up your eyes unto heaven, and see the sun, and the moon, and the stars, and all the adornment of heaven, and be led astray to bow down unto them and serve them, which the Lord your God has allotted unto all the nations under heaven.
But God took you, and brought you forth out of the iron furnace, out of Egypt, to be unto Him a people of inheritance, as at this day.

relationship: close shepherding of Israel in the wilderness
rationale: Hosea says God shepherded the people in an uninhabited wilderness. The psalm likewise describes leading His people like sheep and bringing them up like a flock in the wilderness.
source_text: I shepherded you in the wilderness, in an uninhabited land,

target_units.text: And He led His people away like sheep, and brought them up like a flock in the wilderness,
and guided them in hope, and they did not grow cowardly; and the sea covered their enemies.

relationship: close sequence of fullness, an elevated heart and forgetting God
rationale: Hosea describes the people becoming full, their hearts rising and their forgetting God. Deuteronomy warns against precisely this sequence after food, houses and wealth multiply.
source_text: according to their pastures. They were filled to fullness, and their hearts were lifted up; for this reason they forgot Me.

target_units.text: lest, when you have eaten and are filled, and have built good houses and dwelt in them,
and your herds and your flocks are multiplied, and your silver and your gold are multiplied, and all that you have is multiplied,
you become lifted up in heart, and forget the Lord your God, who brought you forth out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage;

relationship: internal recurrence of God's panther image
rationale: The later warning again compares God to a panther, here adding a leopard along the Assyrians' road. The earlier warning uses panther for Ephraim and lion for Judah; the repeated predator image has different accompanying animals and locations.
source_text: I will be like a panther to them and like a leopard along the Assyrians’ road.

target_units.text: For I am like a panther to Ephraim and like a lion to Judah’s house. I seize and will go away and take, and there will be no one to rescue.

relationship: shared lion-and-bear danger imagery in judgment
rationale: Hosea compares God's encounter to a bear in distress and adds devouring forest lion cubs and field beasts. Amos depicts someone escaping a lion only to meet a bear and then a snake; it supplies a different sequence without saying Hosea's bear lost cubs.
source_text: I will meet them like a bear in distress and tear open their heart’s enclosure. There forest lion cubs will devour them; field beasts will tear them apart.

target_units.text: as when someone flees from a lion and a bear falls upon him, then leaps into his house, braces his hands upon the wall, and a snake bites him.

relationship: close request for a king to judge the people
rationale: Hosea challenges the saving and judging capacity of the king whom the people asked to receive. Samuel records the request for a king to judge and God's response that His own reign had been treated as nothing.
source_text: Where is this king of yours? Let him save you in all your cities; let him judge you, the one of whom you said, ‘Give me a king and a ruler.’

target_units.text: They said to him, “Behold, you have grown old, and your sons do not walk in your way. Now appoint a king over us to judge us like the other nations.”
The word was evil in Samuel’s eyes when they said, “Give us a king to judge us.” Samuel prayed to the Lord.
The Lord said to Samuel, “Listen to the people’s voice in whatever they say to you. They have treated Me as nothing so that I should not reign over them; it is not you they have treated as nothing.

relationship: related divine disapproval of requested kingship
rationale: Hosea says God gave a king in anger. Samuel calls the request for a king a great evil and invokes thunder and rain, after which the people acknowledge their wrong; Hosea's following held-clause is not rewritten as removal of the king.
source_text: I gave you a king in My anger, and in My fury I held

target_units.text: Is it not wheat harvest today? I will call upon the Lord, and He will send thunder and rain. Know and see that the evil you have done before the Lord by asking a king for yourselves is great.”
Samuel called upon the Lord, and the Lord sent thunder and rain that day. All the people greatly feared the Lord and Samuel.
All the people said to Samuel, “Pray to the Lord your God for your servants, and we will certainly not die. We have added to all our sins the evil of asking a king for ourselves.”

relationship: related stored or contained sins
rationale: Hosea's continuing sentence names a bundle of injustice and Ephraim's hidden sin. Job speaks of lawless deeds sealed in a bag; the comparison concerns contained wrongdoing without adding a seal to Hosea's bundle.
source_text: a bundle of injustice. Ephraim—his sin is hidden.

target_units.text: Thou didst seal my lawless deeds in a bag and mark whether I transgressed in anything unwillingly.

relationship: close labor-pain comparison under impending judgment
rationale: Hosea says pangs like a woman giving birth will come upon him. Isaiah likewise describes envoys held by labor pains like a woman giving birth; Hosea's additional unwise-son and crushing clauses are not replaced with a birth-canal interpretation.
source_text: Pangs like those of a woman giving birth will come upon him. This son of yours is not prudent, because he will certainly not endure amid the crushing of children.

target_units.text: the envoys will be troubled, and labor pains will hold them like those of a woman giving birth. They will lament to one another and be distraught, and change their face as to flame.

relationship: close rhetorical challenge to death with distinct wording
rationale: Hosea asks Death about punishment and Hades about its sting. Paul asks death about victory and sting, then gives thanks for victory through Jesus Christ; the addressed names and first object of the question differ.
source_text: I will rescue them from Hades’ hand and redeem them from death. Where is your punishment, Death? Where is your sting, Hades? Consolation is hidden from My eyes.

target_units.text: “Where, death, is your victory? Where, death, is your sting?”
The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.
But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.

relationship: close promise of redemption from Hades' hand
rationale: Hosea promises rescue from Hades' hand and redemption from death. The psalm likewise says God will redeem the speaker's soul from Hades' hand when He receives him; the collective and individual promises differ.
source_text: I will rescue them from Hades’ hand and redeem them from death. Where is your punishment, Death? Where is your sting, Hades? Consolation is hidden from My eyes.

target_units.text: But God will redeem my soul from Hades’ hand when He receives me. Diapsalma.

relationship: related divinely appointed scorching wind
rationale: Hosea says the Lord will bring a scorching wilderness wind that dries channels, springs and land. Jonah likewise describes God commanding a burning, scorching wind, then separately states that the sun struck Jonah's head.
source_text: Because this one will make a division among brothers. The Lord will bring a scorching wind from the wilderness upon him and dry up his channels and desolate his springs; it will dry his land and all his desirable vessels.

target_units.text: As the sun rose, God commanded a burning, scorching wind. The sun struck Jonah’s head; he lost heart, renounced his life and said, “It is better for me to die than to live.”

relationship: close threatened violence against infants and pregnant women
rationale: Hosea announces nursing infants dashed down and pregnant women ripped open in Samaria's judgment. Elisha's prediction concerning Hazael likewise names dashing infants and tearing pregnant women; the comparison does not identify the attackers as the same.
source_text: Samaria will disappear because she opposed her God. They will fall by the sword; their nursing infants will be dashed to the ground, and their pregnant women will be ripped open.

target_units.text: Hazael said, ‘Why does my lord weep?’ He said, ‘Because I know all the evils you will do to the sons of Israel: you will send their strongholds into fire, kill their chosen men with the sword, dash down their infants, and tear open their pregnant women.’

relationship: close call to return to the Lord
rationale: Hosea urges Israel to return because it grew weak in its injustices. Joel likewise calls for turning to the Lord with the whole heart and gives His mercy as the ground; the stated reasons and accompanying actions differ.
source_text: Return, Israel, to the Lord your God, because you grew weak in your injustices.

target_units.text: “And now,” says the Lord your God, “turn to Me with your whole heart, with fasting, weeping and mourning.”
Tear your hearts, not your garments, and turn to the Lord your God, because He is merciful and compassionate, patient and abundant in mercy, and relents concerning calamities.

relationship: close fruit-of-lips language for an offering of words
rationale: Hosea instructs the returning people to take words and promises repayment of the fruit of their lips. Hebrews likewise calls praise a sacrifice and identifies it as the fruit of lips confessing God's name through Jesus.
source_text: Take words with you and return to the Lord your God. Speak to Him so that you do not receive injustice but receive good things, and we will repay the fruit of our lips.

target_units.text: Therefore through Him let us continually offer God a sacrifice of praise, that is, the fruit of lips confessing His name.

relationship: related renunciation of foreign and equestrian security
rationale: Hosea's confession rejects Assur's salvation and mounting a horse. Isaiah condemns reliance on Egypt's horses and chariots without seeking God and declares the helpers unable to stand; the foreign powers named differ.
source_text: Assur will certainly not save us; we will not mount a horse, and we will certainly no longer call the works of our hands “Our gods.” The One in you will have mercy on an orphan.

target_units.text: Woe to those going down to Egypt for help, trusting in horses and chariots because there are many, and in horses, a very great multitude, but not trusting Israel’s Holy One or seeking God!
He Himself, wise, brought evils upon them; His word will certainly not be set aside. He will rise against evil people’s houses and against their futile hope,
an Egyptian human being and not God, horses’ flesh, with no help. The Lord will bring His hand against them; the helpers will grow weary, and all will perish together.

relationship: specific divine care for the orphan
rationale: Hosea declares mercy for an orphan amid the rejection of false sources of rescue. The psalm likewise names the Lord taking up the orphan and widow within its account of His help.
source_text: Assur will certainly not save us; we will not mount a horse, and we will certainly no longer call the works of our hands “Our gods.” The One in you will have mercy on an orphan.

target_units.text: The Lord guards the newcomers; He will take up the orphan and widow, and He will obliterate the way of sinners.

relationship: related healing and restoration with different stated objects
rationale: Hosea promises healing for their dwellings and open love after anger turns away. Jeremiah promises cure from a painful wound, returned deportees and a rebuilt city; the comparison preserves Hosea's dwellings rather than changing them to apostasy.
source_text: I will heal their dwellings; I will love them openly, because My anger turned away from them.

target_units.text: Because I will bring up your cure and heal you from a painful wound, says the Lord, because you were called Scattered: She is your prey, because no one seeks her.
Thus said the Lord: Behold, I will return Jacob’s deportees and have mercy on his captivity. A city will be built upon its height, and the sanctuary will sit according to its judgment.

relationship: related flourishing growth linked with Lebanon
rationale: Hosea promises Israel blossoming like a lily and roots like Lebanon. The psalm compares the righteous to a blossoming palm and multiplying Lebanese cedar; the particular plants and root description differ.
source_text: I will be like dew to Israel; he will blossom like a lily and put down his roots like Lebanon.

target_units.text: A righteous person will blossom like a palm tree; like the cedar in Lebanon he will multiply.
Planted in the Lord’s house, they will blossom in the courts of our God.

relationship: close fruitful-olive image under divine care
rationale: Hosea compares restored Israel to an olive tree laden with fruit. The psalm's speaker likewise compares himself to a fruitful olive tree in God's house and declares hope in God's mercy.
source_text: His branches will spread, and he will be like an olive tree laden with fruit; his fragrance will be like Lebanon.

target_units.text: But I am like a fruitful olive tree in God’s house; I hoped in God’s mercy for ever and for age upon age.

relationship: related shelter and abundant provision described as intoxication
rationale: Hosea promises settlement beneath his shelter and fullness to intoxication with grain. The psalm pairs shelter beneath God's wings with intoxication from His house's richness; the shelters and stated provisions differ.
source_text: They will return and settle beneath his shelter; they will live and be filled to intoxication with grain. His memorial will blossom like a vine, like Lebanon’s wine.

target_units.text: How Thou hast multiplied Thy mercy, God! The sons of men will hope beneath the shelter of Thy wings.
They will be intoxicated from the richness of Thy house; Thou wilt give them the torrent of Thy delight to drink.

relationship: parallel dependence for fruitfulness
rationale: Hosea depicts God as a shading juniper and declares that Ephraim's fruit is found from Him. Jesus uses vine and branches to describe the disciples' dependence on Him for fruit; the different plant images remain distinct.
source_text: As for Ephraim, what has he still to do with idols? I humbled him, and I will strengthen him. I am like a thickly shading juniper; from Me your fruit is found.

target_units.text: Remain in Me, and I in you. Just as the branch cannot bear fruit from itself unless it remains in the vine, neither can you unless you remain in Me.
I am the vine; you are the branches. The one who remains in Me, and I in him, bears much fruit, because apart from Me you can do nothing.

relationship: close concluding question about wise understanding
rationale: Hosea asks who is wise and discerning enough to understand these things. The psalm likewise asks who is wise, will keep these things and understand the Lord's mercies, closing its account with a call to discernment.
source_text: Who is wise and will understand these things, or discerning and will recognize them? For the Lord’s ways are straight; the righteous will walk in them, but the impious will grow weak in them.

target_units.text: Who is wise and will keep these things, and will they understand the Lord’s mercies?

relationship: related contrast of righteous and ungodly conduct through way imagery
rationale: Hosea contrasts righteous walking and impious weakening in the Lord's straight ways. The psalm distinguishes the righteous way known by the Lord from the ungodly way that perishes; Hosea's single set of the Lord's ways and the psalm's contrasting ways remain distinct.
source_text: Who is wise and will understand these things, or discerning and will recognize them? For the Lord’s ways are straight; the righteous will walk in them, but the impious will grow weak in them.

target_units.text: for the Lord knows the way of the righteous, and the way of the ungodly will perish.
